title: Attention fallback resonance benchnotes
content:
Executive summary:

This is a running benchnote of a set of exploratory experiments focused on a repeating production symptom we started seeing in Nov: transient latency resonances when the runtime falls back between attention kernel implementations. Symptom = short bursts (5–50ms) of 95th+ quantile token latency that correlate with kernel-switch events under mixed-sequence traffic. Not the classic steady-state tail; these are high-frequency spikes that show up only when the request mix changes rapidly or when the KV cache hit-rate drops.

Goal:
- Understand the mechanism (why switching triggers oscillatory tail behavior).
- Build a repeatable microbench that reproduces the resonance so we can iterate on mitigations.
- Propose low-risk mitigations (scheduler hysteresis, warm priming, fast quantized fallback).

Why this is different from prior attention notes:
- Prior work focused on single-kernel performance and fusion boundaries. This notebook centers on the _transition_ cost and the transient pipeline effects that persist for a few requests after a switch. We instrumented scheduler queues, kernel priming paths, and memory allocator churn rather than only kernel throughput.

Hypotheses we tested (short):
1) Kernel priming overhead: the first few calls to a kernel after a long idle or after a different kernel incur extra workspace allocations / JIT pathcost.
2) KV-cache warmup: when falling back to paged/ONDemand attention, the KV cache refills slowly so the first tokens do extra PCIe transfers; this cascades into queueing and upstream backpressure.
3) Scheduler handshake: our kernel handoff protocol serializes request metadata updates which create micro-queues; these serialize later operations until the handshake completes.
4) Memory fragmentation and allocator stall: switching changes allocator patterns (different workspace sizes), increasing mutex contention.
5) TensorCore underutilization oscillation: when a kernel swap results in suboptimal kernel selection for a small batch mix, GPU occupancy drops briefly, raising per-token cost and increasing service latency for subsequent small requests.

Test harness design:
- Repro harness run on a single dedicated A10 instance to remove noisy multitenancy.
- Request mixer that emits sequences drawn from a bimodal distribution: short (8–32 tokens) and long (512–1024 tokens) with configurable burstiness.
- Controlled faulting to flip preferred kernel selector after N requests to force deliberate handoffs.
- Instrumentation added: host-side elapsed timers around scheduler handoff; GPU kernel enqueue time; allocator malloc/free counts (per-thread); nvtx ranges and CUDA event timing for kernel priming; PCIe transfer counters sampled via nvidia-smi/pmu where available.
- Metric set: p50/p90/p95/p99 token latency, kernel switch rate, allocator mutex wait time, NVTX priming durations, PCIe bytes per request, GPU SM occupancy averages.

Key experiments and distilled findings:
1) Controlled switch with idle warmup disabled:
   - Repro: fire 200 small requests (short seq) -> force switch to paged/ONDemand kernel -> fire mixed bursts.
   - Observation: first 12 tokens after switch showed ~3x latency vs steady state. NVTX indicates a ~1.6–2.5ms ‘priming’ window where the kernel performs workspace setup. Kernel enqueue to start also shows ~500–700us jitter added.
   - Root cause: workspace allocation + lazy initialization path in the paged implementation (we still defer buffer mapping until first use).

2) High-frequency toggling (rapid alternate small/long sequences):
   - Repro: alternate small and long requests at 10–30 qps, forcing our selector to choose different kernel families frequently.
   - Observation: latency spikes become correlated with allocator mutex contention traces. The allocator (jemalloc wrapper) serialized several threads for ~50–150us per allocation, but because multiple worker threads hit the allocator around the same time the queueing aggregated to 5–30ms spikes at the top quantiles.
   - Root cause: fragmentation and allocation pattern mismatch between fused-op kernel (small workspace) and paged kernel (larger workspace + scatter buffers).

3) Scheduler handshake serialization:
   - Repro: instrumented handshakes; forced a failing fast-path to exercise handshake fallback.
   - Observation: there is a synchronous metadata update path on the critical path for handoffs. When the handoff occurs concurrently across 4–8 worker threads, they serialize on a single spinlock for metadata update, introducing a bursty stall that shows up as a collective 10–40ms kink in request completion times.
   - Root cause: the handoff code updates kernel-affinity maps under a global lock.

4) GPU occupancy oscillation on mixed batches:
   - Repro: run with micro-batches (batch size 1–4) and a small fraction of long sequences.
   - Observation: when the selector switches to a kernel implementation optimized for long sequences, short-batch runs perform much worse on SM utilization for the next few hundred ms. The scheduler does not immediately reselect a more favorable kernel because decision caching has a TTL of 1s.
   - Root cause: decision caching TTL too long for bursty workloads + mismatch between kernel-opt cost model and bursty sequence mixes.

Quick wins and mitigations tested:
- Priming warmup: eagerly allocate typical workspace sizes when a potential kernel switch is predicted (by looking at upcoming queue composition). Reduced the priming window from 12 tokens down to ~2 tokens on average. Tradeoff: increased memory foot-print and slightly higher baseline allocator churn.
- Hysteresis on selector: add a short 200ms hysteresis before switching kernels when past request mix suggests instability. This reduced oscillatory spikes by ~70% without measurable degradation in steady-state throughput.
- Handshake refactor: replaced global lock with per-affinity shard locks and async metadata update (best-effort). This eliminated the collective 10–40ms kink; small residuals remain from allocator stalls.
- Allocator tuning: pre-reserve a small pool of paged-kernel-sized buffers per worker thread to avoid global allocator contention. Lowered allocator mutex contention by ~80% in the microbench.
- Faster fallback path: introduce a pre-quantized, lower-memory footprint variant of the paged kernel (reduced internal buffers, quantized matmul) that has faster priming. Result: falls back cheaper and the spike amplitude is lower. Accuracy/QA risk: need evaluator runs across our known prompt sets.

Longer-term proposals:
1) Selector rewrite to a streaming, lightweight decision engine that uses an exponential moving average over sequence lengths and prioritizes kernel stability for 500ms windows when detected volatility is high.
2) Kernel warm pools integrated with the allocator so switching never triggers a full allocation path. Implement per-GPU warm map keyed by kernel-id + workspace-size bucket.
3) Offload kernel priming meaty work to a background priming thread that can prepare workspaces asynchronously (with cancellation if not used). This would require changes to how we account in the scheduler to avoid charging latency to the wrong request.
4) Add microbench to CI that simulates the bimodal sequence mix and tracks resonance score (new metric) to detect regressions in PRs.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How does networked (multi-GPU) behavior change things? We ran single-GPU tests; cross-GPU handoffs add RPC-level state update that may worsen handshake stall. Next step: repeat on 4x A10 setup with interconnect stressed.
- Does HBM fragmentation persist across long-lived processes? We observed some per-process fragmentation after many switches; need to correlate with long-running Dedicated nodes.
- Evaluate the accuracy cost of the pre-quantized fallback across our eval suite. If quality degrades >0.5% on critical prompts, we need different approach.
- Can we instrument at the kernel runtime level (e.g., counters for kernel microsteps) to get deterministic triggers for priming so we can pre-warm earlier?

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: land handoff lock refactor prototype (PR #872) and post-canary metrics.
- Marco: add per-thread buffer pool prototype; benchmark memory overhead vs latency.
- Lena: run 4x A10 multi-GPU repeat of the key toggles and collect nvlink/PCIe transfer metrics.
- Omar: add the resonance microbench to CI (lightweight mode) and define the resonance score metric.

Appendix: reproducible command snippets (local harness)
- start single-A10 harness (docker): ./tools/bench/harness --device a10 --workers 8 --mixer bimodal --short 8,32 --long 512,1024 --burstiness 0.6
- force switch sequence: curl -X POST localhost:8080/bench/switch --data '{"force_kernel":"ondemand","after":200}'
- collect nvtx traces: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 ./tools/trace/run_nvtx_collector --out traces/priming.nvtx

Notes to reviewer:
- Bench harness and instrumentation are in the perf branch (see linked PR). The changes touch allocator wrappers and scheduler handshake code; please review race/sanity checks carefully.
- If we accept the hysteresis mitigation, we should include an escape hatch controlled by a feature flag so we can toggle behavior in-prod quickly.

End of benchnote.
